# Downloading Library
```{r}
library(fpp2)
library(forecast)
options(scipen = 999)
```

# Data

```{r}
RetailSalesBF <- read.csv("~/Desktop/FALL 2026/BF/data/RetailSalesBF.csv")
sales <- ts(RetailSalesBF$ClothingSalesUSD, start = c(1992, 1), frequency = 12)

# I am taking only the recovery period after the COVID drop since that is a structural change in the plot (May 2020 to Jul 2026)
rec <- window(sales, start = c(2020, 5))
plot(rec, main = "Clothing sales from May 2020")
# The plot shows a big spike every December and a small rise in the level over time, so the data has seasonality yearly probably due to the holiday season.
```

# Differencing for Stationarity

```{r}
ndiffs(rec)
# The output of 1 means the data needs one difference to remove the trend part

nsdiffs(rec)
# The output of 1 means the data needs one seasonal difference to remove the seasonality of yearly pattern

tsdisplay(rec)
# The ACF has a big bar above the dotted blue lines at lag 12 and 24, so the yearly pattern of seasonality is clear.

tsdisplay(diff(rec, 12))
# We can remove the pattern after differencing it but the data is still not stationary but the lag 12 and 24 bars are within the blue dotted lines now. 

ndiffs(diff(rec, 12))
tsdisplay(diff(diff(rec, 12)))
# We will difference regulaary again and now plot looks stationary and almost flat, this is the data we will use for the arima model. 
```

# ARIMA Model

```{r}
auto_fit <- auto.arima(rec, trace = TRUE, stepwise = FALSE)
# We print all the models tried for Arima, we will look at the AIC and BIC and the lower it is the better the model.
auto_fit
attributes(auto_fit)
# From the output we can see the best model is ARIMA(0,2,2)(0,1,0)[12] where (p,d,q) = (0,2,2) and the seasonal part (P,D,Q)[12] = (0,1,0) with a seasonality factor of 12. Since the p is 0 there is no past values from the time series used directly. d is 2 so the data is differenced twice to make it stationary and remove trend. The q is 2 so 2 moving averages are used which two past residuals are taken to do the forecasting.
# Since the P is 0 the model does not look at any previous seasonal values directly. The D of 1 tells us that we use one seasonal difference so the model subtracts the value of the same month from the previous year. Q of 0 means there is no past seasonal residuals taken
# The log likelihood is -538.01, AIC is 1082.02, AICc is 1082.45 and BIC is 1088.36. These scores are used to compare models. Lower is better.
# Since ARIMA requires a lot of data so, since the post COVID period is only 75 months, the model is quite sensitive.
```



# Residual analysis

```{r}
Acf(auto_fit$residuals)
# The bars are mostly withing blue lines, the lag 1 is slightly above so there is a small pattern still seen but no such trend or seaonality.

Box.test(residuals(auto_fit), lag = 20, type = "Ljung")
# The p-value is 0.39, which is above alpha of 0.05. This means the errors look like random noise, and there is no strong pattern left which is a good indicator of model fit and accuracy

plot.ts(residuals(auto_fit))
# The errors are spikining up and going down near the 0 but theres so pattern. The first few recovery months of 2020 have the biggest errors likely due to the recovery period after COVID

hist(auto_fit$residuals)
# The errors are clustered near 0. A few positive value errors make the tail longer on right side.

tsdiag(auto_fit)
# The plots look similar with some errors in a random pattern and bars are mostly within blue lines and the ljung box p values are above 0.05 for most of them.

# Overall, the model errrors are randome and no pattern is seen so the model does well in capturing all the seasonality and trend.
```


# Forecasting the next five periods

```{r}
f_arima <- forecast(auto_fit, h = 5)
f_arima
plot(f_arima, main = "ARIMA forecast, next 5 periods")
# h = 5 means the next five periods which is from August to Dec 2026. The forecast seems to follow similar pattern and depicts small growth from past months. There is a peak in December and slight drop in September that we can see. 
# The blue line shows the forecast. The dark shaded area is the 80% range and the lighter shaded area is the 95% range. The range gets wider because as we predict more and more in the future the accuracy will decrease as we are less sure.
```

# Accuracy

```{r}
accuracy(auto_fit)
# The MAPE is 3.50% which means on average the forecast is about 3.5% away from the actual sales. This is a a rerlatively low percentage of error which means the model is accurate. The RMSE is 1,385 and MAE 845 which show the same error in dollar values. The MPE is 1.45% and ME is 398 which is also small. The Acf 1 is 0.3 which goes with the lag 1 long bar we saw in the residual acf plot so there is some small leftover pattern in the residuals at lag 1. 
```
